character_and_relationship_context: Aminata Diallo is a young woman who lives in a rented room on the outskirts of Bamako, with no running water; she fetches water from a communal stand each morning. She works as a construction laborer, the youngest and only woman on her crew, under master mason Sékou, who calls her 'la petite comptable' because she recalculates load-bearing estimates in her head. She double-checks every measurement, a habit formed after watching her mother lose a market stall due to a miscalculated loan when Aminata was twelve. Her mother died then, and she has been counting everything since: bricks, costs, weeks until her next accounting exam. She keeps a notebook of figures and dates hidden in her shirt and an untouched emergency fund under a loose floorboard. She studies accounting by lamplight at night after ten-hour workdays, saving for a proper room where her younger sister can live and attend school. She does not speak of this plan, because she believes spoken plans can be borrowed against. She walks past food stalls without buying to save money. She has declined three previous social invitations this month to study, citing fatigue, and accepts only invitations that do not require an extra bus fare. Her coworkers respect her silence and precision; she never asks for an advance on her wage. She watched her father sell his tools to pay for a funeral and never hold a trowel again. Sékou has taught her the trade over two years, trusting her with load calculations and once lending her a textbook. His wife has never met Aminata but sends greetings through him.
objective_situation: After a long day at the construction site, as Aminata is packing her trowel, Sékou approaches and says his wife has prepared a large pot of yassa poulet for the neighborhood's Korité celebration. He invites her to join his family for the meal tonight. Aminata is exhausted and had planned to study for her accounting exam by lamplight. She knows that declining a meal invitation during Korité can seem rude, but she also does not want to spend the money on a bus fare across town or the time away from her books. She must decide whether to accept or politely decline.
state_and_available_memories: Aminata's shoulders ache from hauling cement, and her right hand is blistered where the trowel handle rubbed. She has not eaten since a piece of bread at dawn. Her exam notes are tucked inside her shirt, damp with sweat. The smell of yassa poulet reminds her of the last Korité before her mother died, when they ate together at a neighbor's table. Sékou's phrase 'my wife has prepared' echoes the way her mother used to announce a meal. She remembers her mother once refusing a holiday meal because she had to restock the market stall, and later regretting the lost connection. She also recalls that every time she skipped studying to socialize, she felt behind for a week.
name: Aminata Diallo
